title: Michaelmas (29 September)
hook: the feast of Michael and all angels

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holy Cross Day, and a cross honored as a tree. Your line was the tree of life. Which tree did you stop beside? Day one thousand fifty-one.

Some universities still call their autumn term the Michaelmas term. Tradition says older calendars treated the day as a turning point of the year, when accounts were settled. And there's a folk saying, told with a straight face in parts of Britain, that you shouldn't pick blackberries after Michaelmas, because by then they've been spoiled. A feast that ended up in term names and berry picking. Its full name in some prayer books is longer and stranger: the feast of Saint Michael and all angels. Today, Michaelmas.
screen: `A TERM, A SETTLING DAY, A BLACKBERRY RULE.`

segments.voice: Michael is one of the angels the Bible calls by name. In Daniel he is "the great prince" who stands up for his people. The letter of Jude calls him "Michael the archangel." And in Revelation, in a vision, "there was war in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon." So Michael is the angel of standing up, of holding the line. But the feast doesn't stop with Michael. It's for all angels, and plenty of the Bible's angels arrive without swords. In story after story they come as messengers. They turn up with news, with food, with a hand on the shoulder. Which brings us to the carry, from the letter to the Hebrews: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Unawares. Without knowing. Some readers hear in that verse an old story from Genesis. Abraham is sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day. He looks up and sees three men standing near. The text doesn't say he knows who they are. It says "he ran to meet them from the tent door, and bowed himself toward the ground." He brings water for their feet, bread, a calf, milk. As the story goes on, the text has the LORD speaking to Abraham. So the feast holds two pictures. Michael, standing against the dark. And strangers at a tent door, who might be more than they seem. Christians differ in how much they say about angels. Catholic and Orthodox teaching speaks readily of guardian angels; some Protestants say less, and keep close to texts like the psalm: "he shall give his angels charge over thee." On this day, some simply give thanks for help they never saw coming.

Here's the practice: give thanks for unseen help. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last week or so, and find one moment when help arrived that you didn't arrange. Someone held a door, or texted at the right time, or a stranger pointed the way. Maybe you never learned their name. Stay with that moment. Let yourself see their face, if you can. If you pray, you can thank God for that help and for the person who brought it. If you don't, just hold them in mind with thanks. The bell holds the time.
Michaelmas. The feast of Saint Michael and all angels, for the archangel who stands up, and for the messengers who arrive as strangers.
Your line: angels unawares. Today, treat one stranger the way Abraham did: notice them, make a little room, offer something, even just your attention. Day one thousand fifty-one.

howItsDone: Churches that keep Michaelmas read the scriptures of Michael and of angels, and some pray traditional prayers to Saint Michael or about guardian angels; in some places the day also keeps old customs of the autumn.

notes: Claims rule check: the hook's customs (Michaelmas term, settling accounts, the blackberry saying) are not in the cited texts; they are hedged ('some universities', 'older calendars', 'a folk saying'). Cut if a Keeper prefers.
'plenty of the Bible's angels arrive without swords' and 'in story after story they come as messengers' describe the narratives; no etymology of 'angel' is given, per the claims rule.
'some prayer books' and 'some simply give thanks' kept soft per the claims rule.

Editor pass: hedged the old-calendar custom with 'tradition says' and dropped 'the harvest was in' (two days after the harvest lesson), matched the screen line to the voice (no 'rent day' in the voice), softened 'readers hear' to 'some readers', and framed guardian angels as Catholic and Orthodox teaching.

Second editor pass: Genesis 18 never says Abraham failed to recognize the visitors (verse 1 names the LORD), so 'he doesn't know who they are' became 'the text doesn't say he knows', the reveal line now cites the LORD speaking, the myth item claiming he 'didn't know' was replaced with Hebrews' unawares line, and the trapdoor no longer says he didn't recognize them.

Audit pass (fresh auditor, 2026-10-01): fixed a muddled line ('more reserved and point to the psalm' read as if the psalm were an argument against angels); Protestants are now described as saying less and keeping close to the text.
